name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
title: Training Data and Opt-Outs
answer: Training data and opt-outs covers the material used to teach generative models and the mechanisms by which creators ask to be excluded from that use. It sits inside rights and provenance because the same dataset question decides both what a model can produce and whose work is traceable in the output. In practice the topic spans image, video, audio and text corpora, the licences attached to them, and the registries and forms that record a refusal. It is a live subject rather than a settled one, with 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site shaping how the parties behave.

crumbs.name: Rights and Provenance in AI Art

sections.body: Training data and opt-outs covers the material used to teach generative models and the mechanisms by which creators ask to be excluded from that use. It sits inside rights and provenance because the same dataset question decides both what a model can produce and whose work is traceable in the output. In practice the topic spans image, video, audio and text corpora, the licences attached to them, and the registries and forms that record a refusal. It is a live subject rather than a settled one, with 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site shaping how the parties behave.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The underlying machinery is a mix of crawlers, dataset stores, metadata standards and exclusion registries. Web-scale image and text collections are assembled by scraping, then filtered, deduplicated and captioned before training, while audio and video pipelines add transcription and frame sampling. Opt-out signals travel through different channels: robots.txt and similar crawler directives, licence metadata embedded in files, and creator registries that model developers agree to consult. Because these channels are not unified, a single exclusion often has to be filed in several places to have any practical effect.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners approach the problem from two directions. On the data side, teams audit provenance by tracing files back to their sources, checking licences, and building exclusion lists that are applied before a training run rather than after. On the rights side, creators and their representatives document authorship, register works, and submit opt-out requests to the operators they can identify. The two sides rarely share a common record format, so much of the work is reconciliation: matching a creator's catalogue against a dataset manifest and confirming what was actually removed. This site tracks 1,000 live image generation models, 1,000 video models and 2,000 audio models, which gives a sense of how many separate pipelines an opt-out may need to reach.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance here is a patchwork of statute, contract and voluntary commitment. Copyright and related rights set the outer boundary, while terms of service, dataset licences and developer pledges fill much of the middle ground. Courts are actively testing where training ends and infringement begins, and the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, 18 of them involving AI music services, show how much of that question is still unresolved. Provenance tools such as content credentials and watermarking are increasingly used to record where a file came from, though adoption is uneven and no single standard governs all of it. Nothing in this area is settled law, and practice varies widely between jurisdictions and between developers.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more formal records and more granular control. Expect opt-out registries to consolidate, provenance metadata to become a default rather than an option, and licensing markets to emerge for creators who want to permit use on stated terms rather than refuse it outright. Regulators in several regions are moving toward disclosure requirements for training data, which would push documentation practices from voluntary to expected. The open questions are enforcement and scale: whether a small creator's exclusion can be honoured across thousands of models, and whether the courts will settle on a rule that developers can build against.
